item.title: Did a Narcissistic Boss Cost You Your Career?
item.description:
Narcissism

Did a Narcissistic Boss Cost You Your Career?

Five questions that may reveal hidden abuse behind years of self-doubt and shame.

Posted November 18, 2026

Prada was a 29-year-old registered nurse when she came to my office in tears, saying she hated her job and was having panic attacks. Sharon, the hospital’s human resources director, perceived that the trauma exposure in her work in the emergency room was the source of the panic attacks and sent her to specialized resilience training.

Devin, a 42-year-old software architect, came to my office with concerns about depression. He feared losing his job because he was too old and believed that new artificial intelligence programs were replacing him.

At first glance, their struggles seemed understandable, given the unique demands of their professions. The trauma exposure, aging concerns, and technological pressures were real. But more conversations revealed something deeper and more destabilizing: a high-achieving, abusive, and narcissistic boss.

The challenge is that organizations often view a high-achiever as the goose that lays the golden egg, making them revered and supported. But when that high-achiever also commits narcissistic abuse, they can be untouchable. And the fallout of their abusive tactics resides in the long-term wounds of countless victims.

In It's Not You: Identifying and Healing from Narcissistic People, Ramani Durvasula describes how many therapists are trained to address the person’s isolated symptoms and often miss the larger impacts of narcissistic relationships. She also echoes what Lundy Bancroft explained almost 25 years ago in Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men—the abusive person is a master of disguise and actually gains footing with the therapist, while the abused person who shows up as anxious and closed can get further gaslit and retraumatized by the therapist. Moreover, interventions focused on appeasement or better communication can reinforce and escalate manipulation and abusive tactics.

Now imagine that third party is HR, an executive coach, or an organizational consultant.

And imagine that the abusive person is exceptionally accomplished, charismatic, influential, and valuable to the organization.

Who gets believed? Who gets coached? Who gets labeled difficult? And who quietly disappears from the organization?

Given these complex dynamics, I was surprised to read an article in the Journal of Business Ethics suggesting that clear codes of conduct and consequences could help address narcissistically abusive supervision. The authors’ research revealed that leaders high in narcissistic rivalry employ abusive supervision when they perceive employees as deviating from their authority or organizational rules; yet they suggest: “It is essential that organizations recognize the importance of fostering a supportive environment in which both leaders and followers are equipped with the skills and knowledge to interact respectfully with each other” (Gauglitz & Schyns, 2024).

While rules for conduct can establish best practices and delineate what is prohibited, they may fail to address the hidden dynamics of manipulation, coercion, and stealth sabotage.

In Ten Keys to Staying Empowered in a Power Struggle, I explain how manipulative tactics often operate through confusing double-binds, intermittent praise, shifting expectations, selective memory, and gaslighting. These patterns can leave people questioning their judgment while the person causing harm appears credible and composed.

Did Unrecognized Abuse Drive You Out of a Job—or a Career?

I have witnessed people who left jobs—and entire careers—without understanding how an abusive workplace dynamic eroded their confidence, health, and sense of agency.

If something like this happened to you, or someone you know, consider these five questions:

  1. Were you constantly second-guessing yourself on the job? Did expectations change without warning, leaving you feeling that nothing you did was ever enough?
  2. Was praise followed later by punishment? Were you initially valued or celebrated, only to become criticized, excluded, or undermined?
  3. Did speaking up make things worse? Were reasonable questions, concerns, or boundaries treated as personal attacks or disloyalty?
  4. Did you begin doubting your own perceptions? Were events denied, promises forgotten, or blame repeatedly shifted onto you?
  5. Did you lose more than a job? Did the experience affect your confidence, relationships, health, or willingness to pursue opportunities you once loved?

In contrast, healthy workplace dynamics and leadership allow disagreement without humiliation, accountability without retaliation, and growth without diminishing someone's dignity.

Sometimes, recognizing what happened is the first step toward healing, which involves reclaiming what you lost, honoring what you endured, and breaking the cycle of abuse that continues long after the abuser is gone through self-blame, shame, and the transformation of someone else’s cruelty into your own inner voice.

item.title: Finding Solace and Comfort in Listening to Trees
item.description:
Environment

Finding Solace and Comfort in Listening to Trees

Transcending holiday stress and finding rest and renewal in nature.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • As the holidays approach, one way to stay grounded and prevent burnout is to reconnect with natural spaces.
  • Listening to trees is a contemplative and meditative practice that can lead to transcendence.
  • A relationship with nature can heal and sustain us during periods of vulnerability and loss.
  • Transcendence can help us be more deeply engaged with life, promoting connection, meaning, and belonging.

As we approach the holiday season, each of us needs to find ways to take time for ourselves to recover from the activities and responsibilities of the season. Attention restoration theory, proposed by Kaplan and Kaplan (1989), suggests that if we are able to spend time in natural spaces, we can feel rested, renewed, and better able to cope with the stressors and demands of the season. Listening to trees is one healing practice that offers such a possibility by calming the mind and body. Through this practice, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves, where we are in life, how we feel, what is important to us, and what we need during this season.

Listening to trees is one contemplative, meditative practice that invites us to slow down, become more attentive, and be more fully present in our everyday lives. At the same time, spending quiet, contemplative time in natural spaces can lead us to experience feelings of transcendence. Transcendent experiences deepen our sense of connection to ourselves, to the natural world, to other people, and to something larger than our individual lives.

Each person experiences transcendence differently. For some, it is connected to religious beliefs and spiritual practices; for others, it emerges through mind-body practice; for others, creative engagement can lead to transcendence. Experiencing transcendence does not involve the withdrawal from the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Instead, it helps us to be more deeply engaged with life by opening ourselves to a greater sense of connection, meaning, and belonging. Transcendent experiences serve dual purposes. They help us not only to ground ourselves more fully in the moment but also to connect to something that surpasses the immediate moment.

The Comfort of Listening to Trees
Source: Jasmin Tahmaseb McConatha

The Theory of Transcendence

The theory of transcendence (Tornstam, 1977) suggests that as we age, we tend to shift our perspective toward more spiritual and cosmic concerns. According to this view, transcendence includes a shift in meaning by recognizing that time is limited, and understanding and accepting the past while at the same time being more fully in the present. It also includes integrating and accepting all aspects of the self, and placing greater emphasis on connections and relationships (social transcendence), and the well-being of the planet. Transcendence in later life, or gerotranscendence, encompasses all three dimensions and focuses on a deep connection with the natural flow of life, with natural spaces, with the future of the planet, and future generations. As we acknowledge that our time is limited, transcendence can help us heal from loss, cope with bereavement, and navigate day-to-day expectations. Transcendence prompts us to shift our focus more fully to what truly matters, while at the same time connecting us to something beyond our individual lives.

Engaging With Nature

One therapeutic way of promoting transcendence is to regularly engage with nature — to listen to trees. Natural spaces provide solace, comfort, and healing, particularly in later life as aging adults contemplate the world they will leave behind. We also know that our individual well-being and happiness are intricately connected to the well-being of the planet. Listening to trees, walking through forests, spending time in parks and on beaches, or simply viewing nature are all physically and psychologically restorative and healing. The Biophilia Hypothesis (Wilson, 1984) even suggests that our connection with nature and natural spaces is fundamental to our survival. Natural immersion, even a few minutes daily in natural spaces, can also deepen our sensory awareness and draw our attention beyond our worries and anxieties toward a transcendent view in which we reflect on who we are, our place in the world, and what will be left when we are no longer here.

Restorative Blue Spaces
Source: Jasmin Tahmaseb McConatha

Certainly, human beings are not able to survive if nature does not. Our connection to nature is deeply rooted in our biology. Consciously or unconsciously, we have psychological, emotional, and physical connections to the natural world. I first learned about biophilia, our innate human tendency to be connected to nature and living organisms, in graduate school, when I studied the work of psychologist Erich Fromm. Fromm used the term in relation to a love of life and all that is alive (Fromm, 1973). This view has continued to inform my work and my personal life. In my ongoing work on well-being in later life, it has often been evident that our relationship with nature can sustain us throughout our lives, particularly during periods of vulnerability and loss.

Managing Stress

In a culture of haste, in our busy lives, and particularly during the winter holidays, when the days are short and light is limited, burnout is an ever-present possibility. Psychological theories have suggested that if we can find the time to connect with natural spaces during this time, we can manage our stressors and demands more effectively and feel more restored. Attention restoration theory (ART) states that time in natural spaces can replenish our ability to manage our attention, concentrate, and be mindfully present in our daily lives and in our holiday gatherings — and in the process help prevent feelings of loneliness and isolation.

The American Psychological Association has stated that the healing and therapeutic benefits of spending time in natural spaces are available even after only spending two hours each week in nature. By setting aside less than 30 minutes a day to walk, unplug, breathe deeply, and mindfully take in our surroundings, we can begin to experience the restorative energy that nature has to offer. Even limited exposure to nature can be beneficial. Simply viewing nature can have a calming and positive influence on both physical and emotional well-being (Tahmaseb McConatha et al., 2023).

As the holidays approach, one way to stay grounded and prevent burnout is to reconnect with natural spaces. One simple practice is to listen to the trees. This experience can be deepened by finding a comfortable place near or beneath a tree and sitting quietly for a few moments. Even five minutes can help calm the mind and body.

There is no need to find the perfect spot or the perfect tree, or to set expectations or goals for your practice. Instead, give yourself permission to pause, be present, and take in the world around you. Simply engage your senses by noticing the sounds, scents, colors, textures, and gentle movements of nature. Allow yourself to become more aware of your surroundings and embrace the quiet of the moment.

When you are ready to move on, thank your tree for being there and offering stillness, comfort, and a place to simply be.

Renewing transcendence can be a regular practice. It does not require anything other than slowing down, connecting with nature and senses, and allowing ourselves to be fully present.

item.title: When Being the Strong One Makes It Hard to Ask for Help
item.description:
Social Life

When Being the Strong One Makes It Hard to Ask for Help

Being dependable shouldn't mean having to handle everything alone.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Constantly supporting others can lead you to neglect your own needs.
  • Being seen as strong can make asking for or accepting help difficult.
  • True dependability means allowing others to support you too.
Source: Fernando / Unsplash

There's usually someone in every family, friendship group, or workplace whom people know they can count on. When problems in life arise, that person often gets called to support and fix the issue. Can you relate to being that person?

You have probably heard the advice to take care of yourself before caring for others, or "put your own oxygen mask on first". For a lot of people, being the dependable one becomes central to their identity. But sometimes, being the person everyone counts on comes at the expense of taking care of yourself.

Reliability stops being a habit at some point and becomes who you are. You may start measuring your worth by how much you do for others and how little you need from them. Once that's set, asking for help may feel like breaking character.

When Everyone Expects You to Have Your “Stuff” Together

That label, "strong one," can ultimately impact your self-image. It may make it more challenging to reach out when you need support. According to a 2025 review of caregiver experiences, participants reported that individuals, due to the pressure to stay strong and reliable, may feel that they are not living up to their role if they seek psychological help.

You Listen to Everyone, But Who Listens to You?

You may be the person that others call when they need advice or that people turn to when life gets difficult. But when someone asks how you're doing, you change the subject or say “I'm good.”

In a recent 2025 study, experts examined people's beliefs about seeking and receiving help. They found that some people believe accepting help makes them less themselves or threatens their independence. Those beliefs were connected to how people experienced receiving help and to their well-being. Accepting help can be hard, not because support isn't there, but because it can impact how people see themselves.

Why It's Hard to Let Others In

You're probably used to running things and fixing problems on your own. Letting someone support you means admitting what's actually going on, and that gets uncomfortable when your whole identity is built on being the one who handles everything. To engage in vulnerability, try to ask yourself, "When did I last let myself be vulnerable?" Did it bring relief, or did it leave you reluctant to open up again? Letting someone help sometimes means letting go of control and showing them a side they don't usually see.

It can be even harder when you feel pressure to appear "successful" and seem like you have everything under control. For instance, a recent study introduces another factor that can make asking for help difficult: competition. When employees viewed professional success as a contest, where one person's win meant someone else's loss, they were less likely to seek help from colleagues.

How to Get More Comfortable Accepting Help

If you always identify as "the strong one", here are a few ways to become more comfortable accepting help:

  1. Notice when being needed becomes your default role: Pay attention to whether you feel uncomfortable when people don't need your help. Your value in a relationship should not depend on how useful you are to others.
  2. Practice not having all the answers: The next time someone asks how you're doing, let yourself reflect and be honest instead of answering on autopilot. You don't have to turn every hard experience into a lesson or explain how you'll fix it.
  3. Make room for relationships where you can be yourself: Spend time with people who know you for more than what you can do for them. This will hopefully take away the need to always be the strong one or feel that you have to earn your place in someone's life.
  4. Consider talking with a professional: If you find it challenging to express your needs or reach out to people in your circle, mental health support can help you explore those patterns. Online therapy can make it easier to get support and gives you a private, judgment-free space to talk about what you're going through.

Bottom Line

You don't always have to be the person who has it all together. It's okay to have a bad day, ask someone for help, or admit that you don't know what to do. You spend so much time showing up for others that you sometimes forget you need support too.

item.title: How the Film 'Anatomy of a Fall' Can Help You Build Empathy
item.description:
Empathy

How the Film 'Anatomy of a Fall' Can Help You Build Empathy

A film about truth can teach you to see every side of a story.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional empathy means feeling what others feel, while cognitive empathy means understanding it.
  • Research links cognitive empathy to creative achievement in writing, visual arts, invention, and cooking.
  • Empathy builds trust and promotes change, especially in therapy, by helping people gain insight.
  • Parents who empathize with a teen’s need for independence can set boundaries without punishment.
Sandra Hüller in Anatomy of a Fall (2023)
Source: Neon

One of my favorite psychologists and the founder of humanistic psychology, Carl Rogers, saw empathy as one of “the most delicate and potent tools” we have as humans, and definitely not a weakness. The ability to take another person’s perspective and understand their thoughts, feelings, and experiences captures the fundamental meaning of empathy. We can also categorize empathy into two types: cognitive and emotional. In the simplest terms, emotional empathy means feeling what someone else feels; cognitive empathy means understanding what they feel.

The best part of empathy is its accessibility. We are naturally inclined toward empathy, but sometimes we turn it off or shut it out because it we may feel too much and become overwhelmed. It doesn’t have to immobilize us. If that were the case, therapists would never leave the house. We can learn to empathize with and feel for others while still setting boundaries that allow us to get on with our day-to-day lives.

Empathy can serve three key functions in our lives:

(1) Empathy expands our imaginative capacity.

(2) Empathy creates an ethical understanding with another person, creating trust.

(3) Empathy promotes change, especially in therapy, through creating insight.

Creative empathy is essential to our daily life because it enhances our ability to generate new ideas, knowledge, and ways of being in the world. Empathy-building activities in the classroom help students improve their creativity and critical thinking. Empathy can make meaningless activities significant and fun. Empathy helps us see problems from different angles, which can help creative performance.

For instance, a screenwriter must imagine not just what a protagonist wants, but how every character experiences the same moment differently. By empathizing with the different characters’ fears, hopes, and insecurities, a movie avoids clichés, creates richer, more complex characters, and connects better with audiences.

On the other hand, cognitive empathy enhances our ability to understand and express emotions and ideas. Research has found a relationship between cognitive empathy and almost all areas of creativity except science and engineering, where logic and reason dominate. The relationship between creative achievement and empathy shows that cognitive empathy has significant positive effects in visual arts, creative writing, inventions, scientific discovery, and the culinary arts.

Anatomy of a Fall (2023)
Source: Neon

Anatomy of a Fall (2023) is a French film directed by Justine Triet that is an excellent watch for tapping into your creative empathy. If you don’t know the Oscar-winning film, it is an almost Hitchcockian-like thriller that blurs the line between truth and fiction. Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller) is a writer who is put on trial for the death of her husband, whom she claims committed suicide.

As you watch, try these three exercises to tap into your creative empathy:

1. Shift your perspective: Think about how someone else might interpret this situation and Sandra’s character differently.

2. Change your perspective: As you watch Anatomy of a Fall, examine everyone’s thoughts, beliefs, and motivations rather than their emotions. Ask, “What is Sandra trying to protect? What does she believe about truth?”

3. Dive into unfamiliar perspectives: Instead of asking if Sandra is guilty, ask, “What does each character believe happened? Why would that version feel necessary to them?”

Anatomy of a Fall (2023)
Source: Neon

Creative empathy isn't just a luxury for screenwriters, but it's something we all need and crave. We need it to stay flexible, resilient, connected to others, and feel alive. In everyday life, as a parent, you empathize with your teenager’s need for independence rather than control; you may impose fewer rules and reach creative agreements—not punishment or lecturing. In that way, you let them develop the autonomy they need to succeed in life and set compassionate boundaries to help them achieve it.
